title: Small objects in the eye
intro: Dust, sand, eyelashes or tiny metal particles often get into the eye and cause scratching, tearing and redness. Most can be washed out safely. A scratch on the surface of the eye, called a corneal abrasion, can result and is usually painful but heals within days. Some injuries are emergencies.

sections.heading: What to do first
paragraphs: Wash your hands. Do not rub the eye, since rubbing can scratch the surface. Blink several times and let tears wash the object out. Rinse the eye with clean water or sterile saline, tilting the head so that the water flows from the nose side outward. Pull the upper lid over the lower lid to help remove particles.

sections.heading: Looking for the object
paragraphs: In good light, look under the lids by gently pulling the lower lid down and, if needed, rolling the upper lid over a cotton bud. Remove loose particles with a clean damp cotton bud or the corner of a clean tissue. Do not try to remove anything stuck in the eye or touching the coloured part.

sections.heading: Corneal abrasion
paragraphs: A scratch on the clear front surface can cause sharp pain, light sensitivity, watering, redness and the feeling of something in the eye even after the object is gone. Doctors examine it with a dye and a light, and treat it with antibiotic ointment or drops and sometimes pain relief. Most abrasions heal within one to three days. Do not wear contact lenses until it is healed.

sections.heading: When it is an emergency
paragraphs: Go to an emergency department at once if something is embedded in the eye, if the object came from high-speed work such as grinding, hammering metal or drilling, if there is a cut, blood in the eye, vision loss, severe pain, chemical splash or if you cannot open the eye. For chemicals, rinse with water for at least fifteen minutes first and then seek urgent care.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Wear safety glasses for grinding, drilling, woodwork and gardening, and goggles for chemicals and some sports. Remove contact lenses and see a doctor if irritation persists.

examples.title: Helping with a lash
examples.text: Imagine an eyelash is stuck in your eye. You could wash your hands, blink, rinse with clean water and avoid rubbing.

examples.title: Choosing emergency care
examples.text: Suppose a metal fragment flew into your eye while grinding. You might cover the eye lightly without pressing, avoid rubbing and go to an eye emergency department.
